title: Joy in making
hookLine: Ruskin argued workers should be allowed thought and joy in their work (The Stones of Venice, 1853)
carry: a free mind at the chisel

cards: High on an old cathedral, a stone face grins down from a corner, one eye a little bigger than the other, a leaf beside it carved slightly crooked. Not perfect.
The English writer John Ruskin looked at faces and leaves like these and saw something a factory couldn't make: a person thinking while they worked.

In The Stones of Venice, in a chapter called The Nature of Gothic, he argued that those rough edges were not a failure. They were evidence of a free mind at the chisel. Today's word is the man who saw it: John Ruskin.

teach.b: First, Ruskin's choice. He puts it bluntly, in paraphrase: you can make a person into a tool, or you can let them be a person, but you can't do both.
Demand that every cut be exact, every line copied from a pattern, and the hands become a machine, with the mind shut out. Let the worker think, and you'll get mistakes, and also life.
Second, what he saw in the old buildings.
In the carvings he loved, no two were quite alike; each carver was trusted to invent a little. Ruskin read the imperfections as signs of that freedom, something to honor rather than hide.
Third, what he worried about in his own time. The trouble, he wrote, wasn't simply that workers were poorly paid.
It was that they found no pleasure in the work by which they earned their bread, and so looked to wealth as their only way to pleasure.
Division of labor, he said, really divided the worker, leaving each person a small fragment of a task and nothing of their own to put into it. Fourth, why it still lands.
Some jobs hand over a script or a checklist, and some of that is needed; nobody wants a surgeon improvising.
But Ruskin's question is still sharp: is there any room in this work for the person doing it to think, choose and enjoy?
Even a small one: a sentence written your way. The crooked leaf on the cathedral says someone was allowed to make it.

how: Ruskin's chapter The Nature of Gothic is read by students of art, architecture and craft, and is often cited by people who make things by hand when they talk about meaning and freedom in work.

o: an architect who designed Venice's great cathedrals
a factory owner who praised perfect, exact copying
a writer who wanted workers free to think and enjoy

s: Ruskin wanted workers to copy patterns exactly
he argued that demanding exact copying turns a person into a tool.

games.q: you run a building site. your carvers' leaves come out a little different each time. what does Ruskin say to do?
o: make them copy one exact pattern.
let them invent, and honor the differences.
replace the carvings with plain stone.
games.why: Ruskin praised carvings where each worker was free to invent, and read their imperfections as evidence of a thinking person.

practice: Bring to mind a task you usually do by rote, and look at it the way Ruskin looked at a carved leaf. Where could one small piece of you go into it?
Picture adding it, and notice how it feels to be a person in the work, not only its hands; if you pray, you can offer the work in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: John Ruskin, who hoped every worker could think, invent, and take pleasure in what they make, like the crooked leaf carved on an old cathedral. Today's word.
